content: Effective ventilation is the cornerstone of successful neonatal resuscitation. Positive pressure ventilation is typically initiated using manual ventilation devices, which may or may not deliver positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). PEEP has demonstrated beneficial effects in preterm animal models and is widely used in mechanical ventilation within neonatal intensive care units. The objective of this review was to assess whether the use of PEEP during positive pressure ventilation in neonatal resuscitation reduces mortality or morbidity. To achieve this, a comprehensive search strategy was employed. PubMed was searched from 1966 to May 2004 using Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) such as Infant, Newborn, Resuscitation, and Positive Pressure Respiration, along with the text terms Positive End-Expiratory Pressure or PEEP. The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Issue 1, 2004) was also searched using the terms Newborn and Resuscitation. No language restrictions were applied during the search. Additionally, abstracts from the Society for Pediatric Research and the European Society for Pediatric Research (1995 to May 2004) were reviewed, as well as abstracts from journals such as Anaesthesiology, Canadian Journal of Anaesthesia, British Journal of Anaesthesia, Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, and Anaesthesia and Analgesia. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared ventilation devices providing PEEP with those that did not provide PEEP during the resuscitation of newborn infants at birth. The methodology for data collection and analysis included assessing the blinding of randomization, intervention, and outcome measurements, as well as ensuring the completeness of follow-up. The treatment effect was planned to be evaluated using a fixed-effects model, with relative risk (RR), relative risk reduction, risk difference (RD), and number needed to treat (NNT) for categorical data. For continuous data, the mean, standard deviation, and weighted mean difference (WMD) were to be used. An evaluation of heterogeneity was also planned to determine whether pooling of results was appropriate. However, no studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified in this review. As a result, the authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the efficacy and safety of PEEP during positive pressure ventilation in neonatal resuscitation. They emphasized the need for randomized clinical trials comparing positive pressure ventilation with and without PEEP in this context.
